stimulus.text: “I am for doing good to the poor, but I differ in opinion of the means. I think the best way of doing good to the poor, is not making them easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it.” The more public provisions were made for the poor, the less they provided for themselves.
stimulus.source_note: Benjamin Franklin, “On the Price of Corn and Management of the Poor” (1766), abridged. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Benjamin Franklin (1766), abridged, public domain.

books.section: A. Protestant Evangelicalism and Enlightenment Philosophy

primary_sources: Benjamin Franklin, “On the Price of Corn and Management of the Poor” (1766)

stem: According to Franklin, what is the best way of doing good to the poor?

options.text: Leading or driving them out of poverty
Making them easy in poverty with generous public provisions
options.misconception: Franklin says the opposite — making the poor easy in poverty is the way that fails.

options.text: Leaving the poor entirely alone, with no help of any kind
options.misconception: Franklin says he is for doing good to the poor — he argues about the means, not against helping.

options.text: Paying the poor to remain where they are and accept their lot
options.misconception: Paying people to stay poor is making them easy in poverty — the approach Franklin rejects.

rationales.A: Franklin's own words: the best way is not making the poor easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it. Help should move people out of need, not settle them in it.
rationales.B: Making the poor easy in poverty is the approach Franklin argues against, not the one he favors.
rationales.C: Franklin is for doing good to the poor. He disagrees about the means, not about whether to help.
rationales.D: Paying the poor to stay put is making them easy in poverty — exactly what Franklin says fails.
rationales.general:
1. Hear Franklin's aim. He is for doing good to the poor — the question is how.
2. Hear his answer. Not making them easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it.
3. Check the rest. Every other option describes the easy-in-poverty approach he rejects.
Remember: when a writer says “not this, but that,” the answer is the that — read the second half of the sentence.
